Respirometry trials conducted under carefully controlled thermal conditions revealed that the Great Basin pocket mouse exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 28.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 28.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This value, derived from post-absorptive individuals measured during their inactive phase, aligns with the relatively low metabolic intensity characteristic of heteromyid rodents adapted to arid environments. The ability to sustain such metabolic performance at a core temperature of 37.5 °C likely reflects physiological adaptations that balance thermoregulatory demands with the constraints of a granivorous diet in the sagebrush steppe.

Concerning reproductive output, females typically produce litters of 4.8 pups [N_R_i = litters of 4.8 pups] and can achieve up to 1.6 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 1.6 litters per year] under favorable environmental conditions. This annual rate was documented at a mean ambient temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of the species' active breeding season in the Great Basin. The combination of moderate litter size and infrequent reproductive bouts positions this species as a typical equilibrium strategist, investing relatively heavily in each offspring rather than maximizing fecundity.

At parturition, the altricial neonates are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams]. This diminutive size is characteristic of many small-bodied heteromyids and necessitates an extended period of maternal investment in the nest. The pups are born with closed eyes and minimal pelage, reliant entirely on the mother for thermoregulation and nutrition during the initial days of life. A birth mass of 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams] is among the lowest recorded for any heteromyid species of comparable adult size, indicating an altricial developmental strategy that demands high maternal investment.

Adult females of this species achieve an ultimate wet weight of 20.1 grams [Wwi = 20.1 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase from the 1.5-gram birth mass. This substantial growth trajectory reflects the accumulation of body tissues and fat reserves necessary for supporting reproductive effort, particularly the energetic demands of lactation. In field populations, females nearing 20.1 grams [Wwi = 20.1 grams] are typically those preparing for or actively engaged in breeding.

Under conditions approximating the thermal environment of its burrow system at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 5.8 years [am = approximately 5.8 years], a relatively long duration for a rodent of its small body size. Gestation, specific to the thermal regime of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], lasts approximately 24 days [tg = approximately 24 days], a period consistent with the species' altricial developmental mode. The onset of puberty in females occurs at 100 days since birth [tp = 100 days since birth] when reared at a mean temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Finally, weaning, the transition to nutritional independence, is completed at 23 days since birth [tx = 23 days since birth] under similar thermal conditions of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C].
